items.title: Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship
items.summary:
As AI becomes increasingly integrated into legal practice, concerns about its impact remain. “Trust but verify” describes many attorneys’ approach to AI use, according to a new report that also highlights their concerns about job security.

Half of the lawyers surveyed for Bloomberg Law’s AI in Practice report said they trust AI tools enough to use them for complex tasks, and more than 40% said they turn to AI to test legal arguments before asking colleagues.

At the same time, 92% of attorneys said they verify each citation and quotation that AI produces. Many lawyers, including 36% of associates and 22% of partners, said they spend more time correcting AI analysis than doing analytical tasks.

And then there are the fears of AI agents going rogue or replacing humans. Three out of four attorneys said they are at least somewhat concerned about AI agents acting outside their expected parameters. And more than a third of associates (36%) and even 16% of partners fear they will lose their jobs to AI.

State of Practice: Attorneys Rely on AI but Fear Losing Jobs [Bloomberg Law]

The post Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship appeared first on Above the Law .
items.t: Stat(s) Of The Week: An Uneasy Relationship

items.title: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?
items.summary:
(Photo by CRASH:candy/Flickr) 

AI is rearing its head in our courtrooms, and judges are having to decide what to make of it. Two recent decisions show a wrong way and a right way to do just that.

I recently wrote about a federal district court judge in Texas, Mark Pittman, who excoriated some attorneys because he thought they used AI to draft briefs. And because he didn’t like the arguments that they made. He labeled the lawyers lazy and called their arguments tortured. All before holding a hearing. It was my view that this was the wrong way to look at AI and those who use it. 

Then along came an opinion out of the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky. To me, it represents the right and studied way for courts to view AI and its use. The judge there denied a motion to dismiss by a cop who allegedly relied on AI facial recognition, and only AI, to make an arrest. 

The cases are factually different. One involved lawyers using AI, the other a cop. But both turn on the same question: how should a court think about AI and its use by those appearing before it?

The Alleged Kentucky Facts 

A Black man entered a bank in Florence, Ky., and attempted to cash what appeared to be a fraudulent check. The bank refused to cash the check, and he left. A security camera captured an unobstructed view of his face. 

A local police department detective named Kilmer allegedly took a screenshot of the man’s face from the footage. He then used AI facial recognition technology to match that screenshot with a booking photo on file. The cop took the booking photo and a…
items.t: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?

items.title: Many Lawyers Stopped Nickel-And-Diming Clients For Small Expenses
items.summary:
When I first started practicing law, attorneys at the law firm at which I worked needed to enter a billing code to complete many legal tasks. If an attorney wanted to make a telephone call, use the photocopier, or conduct legal research, the attorney needed to enter a client code so that the expense could be tracked and potentially passed along to the client. However, as technology has evolved and competition in the legal marketplace increased, many law firms have stopped charging clients separately for expenses that were once routinely included on legal bills.

One of the most obvious examples of this trend involves telephone charges. Decades ago, long-distance telephone calls could impose meaningful expenses on law firms, and it made some sense for firms to pass these costs along to clients. When I worked in Biglaw, attorneys needed to enter client codes when placing certain calls so that the firm could track the expense. However, most law firms now eat telephone charges rather than pass this cost onto clients, likely because law firms just pay flat rates for this service. Moreover, attorneys increasingly use cell phones and internet-based calling services to communicate with clients and other individuals involved in litigation. Under these circumstances, charging clients separately for routine telephone calls would seem strange, and many law firms no longer bother with such charges.

Photocopying expenses are another area in which law firms have changed their practices. Earlier in my career, attorneys and staff often needed to enter client codes when using photocopiers…
items.t: Many Lawyers Stopped Nickel-And-Diming Clients For Small Expenses

items.title: Federalist Society Judges List Their Hobbies And They’re Total Dorks

Covering the FedSoc National Lawyers Convention , The Hill ‘s Zach Schonfeld (as an aside, check out Schonfeld’s reporting on Alito whining to the conference) posted photos from the event’s “Lunch & SOC!” (cringe) session, where MAGA’s legal auxillary parked a bunch of federal judges at tables so they could bond with attendees over their outside interests, presumably while munching on Chick-fil-A. Something went awry with the signage because rather than neatly printed placards, some of these have strips of posterboard haphazardly cut and pasted onto the signs, like a ransom note.

But, friends, we’ve got to talk about how absolutely miserable it must be to dine with most of these people:

Honestly, the venue probably had real scissors if you’d asked! (Photo by Zach Schonfeld via X)

It should go without saying that “America” is not a hobby. items.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket , which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s…
items.t: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

items.title: Judge Is Done Playing Nice With DOJ Over The Broadview Six
items.summary:
Judge April Perry has spent months trying to get a straight answer about what happened in the grand jury room in the Broadview Six case. The Department of Justice has spent those same months getting more and more creative about making sure she never gets one.

This week, Perry ran out of patience.

Quick refresher. Six protesters, including former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, were charged with felony conspiracy over a September 2025 protest outside the Broadview ICE facility in suburban Chicago. The case fell apart spectacularly in May , when prosecutors dropped all charges after Perry got a look at the grand jury transcripts. The transcripts showed that the first grand jury refused to indict, returning a “no bill.” So the prosecutor kept at it. She vouched for the case, talked substance with grand jurors outside the room, and excused the ones who disagreed with the government, until a later panel finally gave her the indictment. Perry said at the time, “I have never seen the types of prosecutorial behavior before a grand jury that I saw in those transcripts.” Then there’s the matter of what U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros knew and when, which didn’t exactly help his office’s credibility .

So Perry scheduled a hearing and asked Boutros and three line prosecutors to explain themselves. DOJ sent in Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward ( who has been making quite the name for himself this administration ) to make sure that never happens.

First, Woodward claimed that communications with the local prosecutors were privileged and off-limits to Perry’s inquiry.…
items.t: Judge Is Done Playing Nice With DOJ Over The Broadview Six

items.title: Cahill’s Chair Insists The Firm Is ‘Strong’ As Merger Talk Swirls

Ed. note : Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day . 

From our perspective and by any objective measure, Cahill remains incredibly financially strong, highly profitable, with a leading market position. The people driving the firm’s strong results remain fully committed to the firm. 

We do not love departures, of course, nobody does. We feel very confident in the core people who drive the most important practices at the firm. 

— Herb Washer , chair of Cahill Gordon & Reindel, in comments to Bloomberg Law , responding to reports that another firm may acquire Cahill . Washer said Cahill is “regularly approached by other firms in the market for a variety of reasons,” but added, “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on rumors or speculation.” The firm has lost eight finance partners this year, about 10% of its partnership, even as it reported $502.5 million in revenue and $5.7 million in profits per equity partner in 2025. In September, Washer told Bloomberg Law that Cahill expected double-digit growth in 2026.

items.title: Richard Blumenthal Humiliates Grandstanding Texas U.S. Attorney With Remedial Constitutional Law Lesson
items.summary:
When the Trump DOJ openly adopted a bunker mentality , urging U.S. Attorneys to be “prepared for full-on battle” in the wake of the administration’s midterm shellacking, it was really just a matter of time before one of those thirsty MAGA careerists would concoct a publicity stunt to ingratiate themselves to the their DOJ bosses. That said, a Texas prosecutor threatening a Connecticut senator over something happening in Washington wasn’t on anyone’s bingo card.

So you’ve got to give Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, full credit for creativity!

Reitz kicked off his ill-advised assault on Wednesday, writing Senator Richard Blumenthal “to formally give you notice of your obligation to preserve all documents, communications, and other electronically stored information relevant to your intent to deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights to violation of 18 USC §§ 241 and 242.” 

Blumenthal, the ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has written donors to Trump’s ballooning White House ballroom slush fund , asking how much they gave and whether they got anything in exchange for their “donations.” Reitz fired off his letter claiming Blumenthal “threatened citizens for associating themselves with the President and other public officials.” 

Reitz promptly posted the letter on X, in case you were thought for even a second that this was remotely serious. But you’ve got to feel for Reitz… it must suck to snivel your way through the Federalist Society cursus honorum all the way to U.S. Attorney just to watch…

items.title: Calling A Judge A ‘C*cksucker’ Is Rude, But It Isn’t Criminal Contempt
items.summary:
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has some news for thin-skinned trial judges: being called a cocksucker from the gallery is crude and impolite… and not, as it turns out, a crime.

Back in June 2022, Basile Outlaw was sitting in Philadelphia Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington’s courtroom to support a friend facing criminal charges. When Judge Covington denied the friend’s motion to suppress, Outlaw stood up and said that “the judge is a cocksucker,” loudly enough for her to hear it. Judge Covington asked, “What did you say?” Outlaw had a sudden flash of good judgment, said, “Never mind. I’m leaving,” and walked out.

A deputy sheriff and a court employee searched the building for him. He came back on his own to apologize, saying he regretted the outburst, and was taken into custody for direct criminal contempt. Outlaw was sentenced to, and served, 30 days in jail for the offense.

On appeal, the Philadelphia District Attorney’s Office agreed with Outlaw that there wasn’t enough evidence to support the conviction, but the Superior Court upheld it anyway. That left the Supreme Court without anyone to argue for the conviction, so it invited the state Attorney General’s office to do it, which it accepted.

In an opinion by Justice David Wecht, the Supreme Court unanimously reversed the conviction. To prove direct criminal contempt in Pennsylvania, the Commonwealth has to show misconduct in the court’s presence, committed with intent to obstruct the proceedings, that actually obstructs the administration of justice. And obstruction means a significant disruption. In the…
items.t: Calling A Judge A ‘C*cksucker’ Is Rude, But It Isn’t Criminal Contempt

items.title: Tribal property and the Supreme Court
items.summary:
One of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock ) , Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “ atmosphere ” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

Before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP ), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline company. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

Though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in…
items.t: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

items.title: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype
items.summary:
Most revolutions in legal technology rely on the next generation to come in and save the seasoned Luddites from themselves. From desktop computers to the internet, it’s the incoming lawyers who performed the heavy lifting while the senior partners continued printing out emails and sending handwritten replies through interoffice mail.

But as the legal industry dreams of its AI-native future, the next generation of lawyers are a lot less psyched about the technology’s potential. While firms allocate millions ( if not a billion ) to developing AI tools to take work from the first touch to fully drafted work product, college students don’t trust AI much beyond a fancier research tool.

“The College Student AI Reality Check,” is a new report from Blickstein Group reflecting responses from students across 37 colleges and universities, plus five in-depth interviews. Spearheading the report was Vera Grabow, the group’s intern and a college junior double majoring in History and Political Science, who launched the project based on her own experience watching AI reshape her education and recognizing that no one had actually asked students what they thought about the technology that every press release breathlessly proclaims to be the future of work. “She conceived this project, convinced us to undertake it, wrote the questionnaire, lead the outreach, analyzed the data, and drafted the report,” CEO Brad Blickstein said. “We helped, but this was an exceptional piece of work by a college student.”

She favored policies that did not curry his favor, such as expansion of health care coverage, and advocating the release of the Epstein files. 47 then took after MTG . She spit out the Kool-Aid. Finally, after years, in fact, decades of elder statespeople clinging to their seats, clueless about the state of their constituents’ worlds, many of them received well deserved boots back to their home states. Instead of retiring with dignity, they suffered ignominious defeats. The Hill called it a “ youth quake .” Whatever you choose to call it, it was long overdue.

More than 40 nonincumbent millennials won seats. Gen Z representation tripled. As a dinosaur lawyer (and voter), I am delighted to see that new ways of thinking, creating, and innovating may help how we are governed going forward. While there is certainly value in institutional memory, that memory dims with time’s passage.

A headline in one of the post-slaughter articles of the midterms read (and I am paraphrasing here), that 47 didn’t learn anything. Really? items.title: The Itty Bitty Sh*tty Committee

Recently, I was invited to dinner with a group of highly accomplished and well-respected women general counsel. I was genuinely excited. It was an opportunity to meet women I admired, hear about their experiences, and learn from them.

Before the dinner, I did what many of us do: I researched the other attendees.

As I read their impressive biographies, I noticed something. I was the only attorney attending who had never served as a general counsel.

I registered that fact and went on with my day.

Or at least I thought I did.

That evening, after spending the day at a professional conference that should have reinforced my confidence and reminded me of my own experience and accomplishments, I got ready for dinner. Most of us know that committee in one form or another.

You’re not a partner at your firm.

items.title: Judge Richard Posner, The Model Of A Scholarly Jurist, Dies At 87
items.summary:
Richard Posner wrote more than 3,300 opinions over nearly 36 years on the Seventh Circuit . He also authored or co-authored over 50 books and published something like 900 journal articles. According to one accounting, Posner averaged 14.7 articles per year over the course of 62 years. He’s the most cited legal scholar of the latter half of the 20th century . Judge Posner died this week in Chicago. He was 87.

One could focus on all the absurd numbers Posner racked up throughout his career. As one of the leading lights of the Law and Economics philosophy, he’d probably find it amusing to see tributes casting his legacy into something fixed and quantifiable. Yet, as the legal community honors Posner’s memory, the outpour of personal and professional anecdotes highlights the limits of a philosophy seeking to turn the world into a series of ticks on a ledger. 

Our founding editor, David Lat, put it simply :

I am so, so sorry to learn of the death of Judge Richard Posner. I was honored to call him a friend.

Above the Law and Judge Posner enjoyed a long and delightful relationship. Lat once asked, not entirely joking , whether Posner was the Beyoncé of the federal bench. Posner responded to the suggestion that “I am so pleased to be classified as a mono-monikered visionary.” He gave us interviews , benchslaps to write up, and a cat to run for president. Not sure that last one was constitutional. On the other hand, neither is running for a third term, and no one seems prepared to put a stop to that right now . 

I never spoke with Judge Posner myself, but that doesn’t mean I…

items.title: 50 Ways To Do Well In Law School
items.summary:
Law school can make accomplished people feel incompetent by lunchtime. You arrive with good grades and ambition. Then someone asks you to explain a nineteenth-century opinion, challenges every answer, and moves on before you understand what happened.

Your response may be to read every case twice and spend Saturday making your outline beautiful. That can leave you exhausted without making you better at the work your exams require.

Doing well takes a more deliberate approach. You need to understand the material, apply it to unfamiliar facts, and explain your reasoning under pressure. These 50 habits can help you succeed in class and prepare for your career.

Build a Workable Routine 

1. Read the syllabus closely. Put deadlines, exam dates, and assignment weights on one calendar. Learn the attendance and participation requirements before an avoidable mistake costs you points.

2. Schedule specific work. Replace “study torts” with “answer two negligence hypotheticals.” A defined task gives your afternoon purpose and tells you when you’refinished.

3. Protect your best hours. Do difficult reading and practice problems when you are most alert. Save administrative tasks for the part of the day when your attention fades.

4. Leave room for disruption. A schedule that assumes perfect concentration and no interruptions will collapse. Build in time to catch up before one difficult week becomes three.

5. Measure what you can do. Hours in the library tell you little. Ask whether you can explain a rule, recognize an issue, and write a useful analysis.

items.title: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process
items.summary:
One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “ to be more fully informed .” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions? 

As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not…
items.t: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

items.title: What Trump cases might soon return to the Supreme Court?

During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats on two of his signature initiatives – his efforts to limit birthright citizenship and impose sweeping tariffs – as well as his initial attempt to fire Lisa Cook , a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those issues. In the wake of the court’s decisions in each of the three cases, Trump continues to fight on, which has led (or could lead) to litigation that may reach the court again.

The Democratic Party’s decisive victory in the midterm elections, which gave it a majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, could theoretically hinder Trump’s plans. However, Democrats would need not just a majority to pass legislation curbing the president’s authority but a veto-proof majority: 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House, which could be more difficult to obtain.

items.title: Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards showed a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

The constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article I of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

items.title: Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution
items.summary:
A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)” 

***

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s new book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

First, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark , which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.)

But Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer…
items.t: Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution

The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics , holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision…

items.title: Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court
items.summary:
The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”

Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the  National Capital Planning Commission  and the  Commission of Fine Arts  could review the plans for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and said that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. items.title: Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline
items.summary:
The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. left little doubt about how the justices will resolve this one: they seem unlikely to hold that the gas company condemning land for a federally approved pipeline should have to pay attorneys’ fees that the United States would not have to pay if it condemned the land directly.

The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act ’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines. When the federal government approves such a pipeline, the Natural Gas Act allows it to acquire the land in which to build the pipeline or leave that to the gas company. In either case, if the landowner does not agree, a suit exercising the federal government’s right of eminent domain can force a transfer of the land for a “necessary right-of-way,” so long as the landowner receives the “ just compensation ” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.”

The landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline company rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution. In particular, North Dakota law well might require the company to pay the attorneys’ fees of the landowners.

The justices, though, were having none of it. The air was redolent with skepticism from the moment Robert McNamara rose to press the landowners’ view. Justice Clarence Thomas started off by asking – doubtfully – whether “if the U.S. delegates its power … of eminent domain, you’re saying that it…
items.t: Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

Earlier on Monday, the justices heard arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe , on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc . , on whether the “ just compensation ” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

items.title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue border wall construction
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion , the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. items.title: Mahmood’s ICE-style immigration raid agency accused of ‘fishing expeditions’
items.summary:
Exclusive: Almost two-thirds of visits lead to no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant

Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in “fishing expeditions” after figures disclosed that almost two-thirds of enforcement visits result in no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant.

The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration.

There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests.

Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence.

Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

items.title: Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend . These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review . Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

The businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

items.title: Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards
items.summary:
Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards , that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging…
items.t: Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards
